utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I remind you, sir, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when we left off on Friday, you said you saw Mrksic and then went to the barracks, where you met Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic. And you said you weren't sure but you might have gone home at that point, after meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably didn't go home. I don't remember what I did exactly; that was 15 years ago. I met them over a coffee. I talked to them. I told them I had been to see Mrksic about the Vojnovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Vujanovic"] request and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you have certain things that you had to do at home on that day that would have required you to go home?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at home. There was no one back home. My family were in Serbia and my house was empty. I practically didn't even go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness see Exhibit 156, please, it's a map. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is something about the transcript page 1, line 22, it says Vujanovic, whereas the witness said Vojinovic. Mrksic and Vujanovic, it's quite a material error.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to that spot --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. [Interpretation] I'm really sorry, it's not Vojinovic, that's a different person. Vojnovic without the I. Vojnovic is the man in question here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you confirm that, please, Mr. Weiner with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what I was planning to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The two people that you met at the entrance to the barracks, could you state both of their names, full names, first and last, slowly for the transcriber to type them into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, do you see the map in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you claim that you met with Colonel Mrksic at Negoslavci. Could you use the pen, with the usher's assistance, and put a circle with a 1 next to the place or the area where you claim to have met with Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you mark that with a 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then from there you said you went to the barracks next. Could you put a 2 --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if I went to the barracks or to Velepromet first. I can't remember exactly. It could have been either one that I went to first. The barracks is further down, this point right here, not really showing, but where I put the number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then could you show us where your home was. You're not sure if you went to your home next.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My home -- my home -- my home is about here, thereabouts, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there's a 3? Thank you. And finally could -- could you put a circle around the area of Velepromet where you eventually attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And a 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'd like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 772, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you have no records or diary for that particular date - isn't that correct - of November 20th?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on Friday at page 11.951 when you spoke of that time of day, the morning up to the noon time, you said that you couldn't be specific because it was 15 years earlier. So your time as to your meeting with Mr. Vojnovic you said give or take an hour or two. Isn't that correct? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was before the meeting, but I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after you met with -- when you met with General Mrksic you don't know who met with him after you, do you? You can't tell us who he met with after --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Nor can you tell us who he spoke with later that day, after meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I did not meet Mr. Mrksic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you don't know who he was on the telephone with, if anyone, on that date?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were familiar with Colonel Panic, who you said was the Chief of Staff to Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that the Chief of Staff works very closely with the commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know on that date Colonel Panic as Chief of Staff would have had a closer working relationship to you, who was a civilian on that date, and we're talking closer working relationship to Colonel Mrksic than you would because you were a civilian on that date. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you weren't present for any discussions that Colonel Mrksic had with Colonel Panic on that date, were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had just passed the information on to him and then I went straight back and I didn't see Mrksic again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified on Friday that you didn't attend the entire meeting on the 20th, the entire session. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was there for part of the session, but not the entire session. Or perhaps -- perhaps I had entered the hall before the meeting, just before the meeting, just partially -- or actually, I can't remember how long I was there for, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you don't even recall if you stayed until the end of the meeting. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. What I do remember is that probably as I was passing the barracks I was probably on my bay to Petrova Gora to tell them that Goran Hadzic would attend. So it was probably that. As I was passing the barracks to tell them that Goran Hadzic was there. Probably that was that. Probably that was the reason, when I was passing the barracks on my from Velepromet, that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you think you went to the barracks and then to notify people in the --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, when I -- Petrova Gora. The neighbourhood, Petrova Gora, that's approximately where my house was, it was a large neighbourhood, that was the Petrova Gora detachment logistics. I was there to tell the people that Goran Hadzic would be there to see them. And the barracks is in a "defiles" just next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now -- now, you were not present at that session for any conversation between Goran Hadzic and Colonel Panic, were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware of any conversation that Colonel Panic had with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that Colonel Mrksic told Colonel Panic that the trial of the prisoners would be as they decided that session? Would that have surprised you to learn that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. I wish to object about this sort of question. I really don't think that the witness can be asked this kind of question, especially in this context, nor is the witness in a situation to answer questions what would have been if a witness that the Prosecutor has mentioned had told anything to Mrksic. He already told us everything that he knows about the meeting with Mrksic and he said he knew no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree that is the evidence of the witness, but the Prosecutor is entitled to put another version of the facts to him and to get his reaction. In fact, it may well be that he is obliged to do that, to disclose firmly his position. So carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were not aware of that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said the last time around, Vukovar had no electricity and no running water at the time. We had no TV. We couldn't follow what was going on, no interviews by officials or dignitaries, none of the developments in Serbia, Croatia, or the world for that matter. We were in isolation. We had no information incoming or outgoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would it surprise you that some hours or several hours after Velepromet meeting soldiers from the local units and detachments took custody of those prisoners at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Surprised -- I don't know. I don't know whether this was then. I didn't know about that. I had no authority to do anything, take any steps. I wasn't interested in that at all. I had enough of my own worries. I thought this had all been organised, that this had all been resolved, and that there was nothing contentious about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you do know that they were murdered shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another area and then we'll get back to some of these other matters. Just very briefly, on Thursday and Friday of last week you discussed with the Court or you testified about being the chief of security. You discussed -- you testified about that Thursday and then on Friday, earlier?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war -- before the war, before the combat operations, the chief of the Vukovar TO brigade -- before the war when the TO brigade was still unified within the armed forces of Yugoslavia. But can I just make one correction, please, you asked me on Friday the following question if I would have been willing to carry out any order that Mrksic could have given me. I said yes. What I meant was combat orders. Even the most difficult combat order I would have been perfectly prepared to carry out. What I would not have carried out is anything that was outside the Geneva Conventions or any sort of war crime. That is understood. I would have carried out no such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, you testified that when you served as a chief of security you served according to the JNA's rules and doctrine. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but that was in peacetime. It was a peacetime brigade. At this time there was no war operations going on. This was just a drill to see how tactical assignments could be carried out, but this was not a real wartime situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified that you were commanding the military police elements, and that's the phrase you used, "commanding the military police elements." Isn't that what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the war when I was already working with the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what position did you hold when you were commanding the military police elements?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was when I became assistant chief of the brigade for command and staff affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And so as assistant chief of security you were commanding the military police elements and you were issuing orders to them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, directly, just me. I used some elements but personally the chief, the commander, they were the ones who could have given orders personally. Some elements with less structure, yes, I was allowed to give orders and to organise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said you, also on that same page on 11928, that you were issuing assignments to commanders of certain squads. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not detachments, company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read it. Line 19. "I was issuing assignments to the commanders of certain squads when needed. I had the authority to do this." So you were issuing commands to company commanders, too?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then this is definitely misinterpretation. I was a detachment commander with company elements in it. There were no other detachments that I could have been in command of, just the one, the Petrova Gora TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is while you were the assistant chief of security. You said while you were the assistant chief of security: "I was commanding the military police elements. I was issuing them orders. I was issuing assignments to the commanders of certain squads when needed, so I had the authority to do this." That's what you testified to on Thursday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that was in 1993 and 1994. This is not what we're here about. When I took up that job with the corps after the war, that's when it was. That was three or four years after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is -- we're just getting off of Vukovar for a moment, is: Were you in fact issuing orders to the commanders of certain squads when you had to, and you had the authority to do this, and you had your job two years later and three years later, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just elements of the police force, but no real assignments or orders -- you mean bringing people in, mobilising people? I'm not sure what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified on page 11928: "I was issuing assignments to the commanders of certain squads when needed so I had the authority to do this." And then the question says: "Thank you." And then you continue: "Of course with the approval of the commander." So my question is: At the commander's request, did you issue assignments to commanders of certain squads?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as it was security related, in terms of security for command facilities, bringing persons in, that sort of thing, but nothing apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when the commander asked you to or assigned you to a certain task, you would have the authority to issue orders to complete that task. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing. Only if a task was in the spirit of our rules and regulations. The international law on war and the Geneva Conventions, but nothing else outside that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that it was anything outside the Geneva Conventions, sir. Don't worry about that. Now, you testified on Friday that criminals were being appointed to military positions. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall saying in a when Mr. Sljivancanin's counsel said operative work was done in relation to me, if Mr. Sljivancanin and his counsel could please tell us more about the results of that bit of operative work. When they say operative work, what exactly was this about and what results were obtained? Can they reveal this so we can have it all out and see what the results were, who was right in the end, and what the purpose was of all this operative work being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just handle the question and we'll take it one step at a time. But you indicated criminals - and I'm using criminals that was your word - had been appointed to certain positions in Vukovar in 1991.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If after the war someone obtained a profit amounting to millions of German marks and prior to the war they had nothing, nothing at all, then that would certainly leave me wondering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I think the Prosecutor is here misleading the witness to some extent. What the witness has been talking about and what the Prosecutor is asking him, he was talking about the Croatian MUP in Vukovar 1991 prior to the clashes took place when the HDZ took power. I think the witness's words were uttered in that context. Now the Prosecutor is trying to put this in a different context, view it in a different light and misrepresent the situation, and use it to seem as if these things were happening in October. I think this is strictly speaking out of context. I think the witness was initially speaking about these developments at the time when the HDZ took power and tried to re-organise the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The context of the conversation concerned his not being appointed, allegations of auto theft, allegations of war profiteering, and it concerned criminals in general, where this man he claimed he was honest, he didn't make any money, but others were smuggling cars. And the acts of others he has said many times were being attributed to him and he came under investigation. So he's speaking in terms of the criminal activity at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the issue that may require some exploration, Mr. Weiner, in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were just talking -- speaking in terms of people making money in profits. You mentioned large amounts of German Deutschmarks at that time. Were these illegal activities which were occurring, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what these illegal activities -- what legal activities might have been used to create such a huge wealth over such a short period of time. It was probably some sort of business, oil or whatever. I'm not sure if all the papers were in order, but people were brought to these positions and one thing I don't understand is that a person with next to no education or training all of a sudden becomes a boss, as people where I come from normally call that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned allegations of fraudulent activity such as car smuggling. Was there car smuggling or car theft occurring at that time in Vukovar in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should ask the chief of security of that area, Mr. Sljivancanin, he was in charge of operative work and it was his duty to present the results and the fact. There was operative work being done about car theft, then he should tell us who the thieves were, how this was organised, what the profit was, and who had come up with the whole idea and who the possible perpetrators could have been. My function was a command function, I was not in charge of any security matters nor was I into that sort of thing. As a matter of fact, I had no time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I was just interested, sir, in your awareness. Were you aware that people were stealing cars, smuggling cars at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't interested in anybody else's intrigues or hearsay. I wasn't that sort of person. I wanted facts. I wanted proof. If I had hard evidence, then we could talk about it; if not, well, I just didn't press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you indicated you were upset about false allegations being made against you and you testified that the crimes of others were being attributed to you. What crimes are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke when I said a crime. What I wanted to say, what I had in mind, was guilt and what I was implying is that somebody pointed a finger at me. If there was operative work done, then it had to be done covertly. Operative work is normally done covertly so that other people don't know about it. And if they had some final conclusions, then they ought to have tried me, they ought to have prosecuted me. And to wage that campaign, to attribute to me something that was done by other people in order to throw dirt on my name and to bring me down and to shift the blame from other people who were actually guilty and who should have been subject of operative work, and then those people ended up being rewarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What type of crimes, sir, were being attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes such as trafficking, trade with stolen vehicles, and also putting claims that I had large sums of money deposited in Sabac bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were other people committing those types of crimes? Not yourself but others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, but it wasn't my business to keep track of it and I wasn't looking for that type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 353, please? The second page in the become, page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, sir, the line is on the first column -- there's three columns. The first column on the left, the -- it looks like it's the first sentence, the second sentence, the words [B/C/S spoken]. In English it would be: "The volunteers who had come from Serbia and other parts belonged to different groups such as adventurers who would come to experience the turmoil of war, looters, and robbers." Were you aware that those types of people had arrived and were in Vukovar in the fall of 1991, these looters and robbers, and adventurers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there were such cases, but not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were aware, sir, that there was soldiers in Vukovar in the fall of 1991 who were quite dangerous, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like everyone else, there were calm people, there were people with a short fuse, just like in peacetime. You know, people have different attitudes and in wartime, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you were advised -- sir, according to your testimony in Belgrade at page 88, you were advised that they were preparing for your execution. That's what you testified to in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you further indicated in your interview to an investigative judge that a security officer had warned you that they were preparing to liquidate you. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers from the Vukovar barracks who were active officers in the barracks before the war and who were on good terms with me informed me via my brother that there would be an attempt on my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was trying to liquidate you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know who was involved. Once or twice in Velepromet I barely managed to stay alive. Once a sniper bullet zoomed past the back of my head and on the other occasion it was just in front of my forehead. So on two occasions they tried to kill me with a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"? Were these members of your detachment, TO members?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I didn't know that actually -- or actually, I don't know it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you believed the threat to be serious and credible, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and that was proven later on by what happened afterwards. Another thing that happened to Miroljub Vujovic in Petrova Gora where there was a meeting. I later analysed that. He was with people he had come with, and when he informed them of the order issued by Sljivancanin, he was really monitoring me closely to see what would my reaction be. Had I objected, he would have definitely shot me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said that first -- it was proven later by what happened afterwards. Are you referring to those two sniper incidents? Is that what you mean by what happened afterwards? Are you referring to the Ovcara murders? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Petrova Gora when a meeting was held there, Miroljub Vujovic and several other people were there with me. So there were no people of authority there, no people with good reputation, no honest and good people. I think there were three of them. And in that meeting I was able to see what the situation was like. He irritated me, tried to provoke me. I took it all calmly because I knew that I mustn't object because I knew what would ensue had I objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who did you indicate previously in the paragraph was monitoring your activities and you felt that they would have shot you if there was a problem? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To shoot? What do you mean? I'm not sure which paragraph you have in mind. I don't remember that particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You just testified: He was with people he had come with when he was informed of the order by Sljivancanin. He was really monitoring me closely to see what my reaction would be. Had I objected, he would have definitely shot me." Were you referring to Miroljub Vujovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's what I stated just a minute ago. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that the people -- with regard to the people in Vukovar in the fall of 1991, that it was possible to shoot or murder someone. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once everyone is issued with a weapon, it's very hard to maintain law and order, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as a result of these threats, you withdrew completely from the TO and especially you withdrew after learning of these plans to liquidate you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that both on Friday and today and also on Thursday the witness explained several times why he had withdrawn, and I don't see why the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, please avoid giving your version of the facts. The witness is very capable of putting correctly the position, if it's wrongly put to him by the Prosecutor. There's no sign of him being overawed or confused. So we leave the cross-examination to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, after learning that someone was trying to prepare a plan of liquidation for you, that was a reason for you to have withdrawn -- or that was why -- one of the reasons for you withdrawing from the TO and the detachment and basically military life?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after that you had little, if any, contact with the TO leaders Vujanovic and Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following that, no contact whatsoever. And it was only after Krajina fell that, since I was at this headquarters and I was deputy commander for logistics, and it was only written contact, people whom he had sent to me to the headquarters that he had mobilised, I sent those people back. But I had no direct contact with him. It was only in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you last met Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic at the barracks entrance on the 20th. Now, in your statement to the investigative judge in Novi Sad you mentioned that meeting and you state on page 7 in the English, which is the Novi Sad investigative judge interview of 2003, and in the B/C/S on page 0299-2269, which is the fourth paragraph up from the bottom in the B/C/S, in the English the last paragraph. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statement of Captain Radic, not my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, this is the B/C/S statement 02992269. It's in the folder, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please remind me which --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's in the folder to your left. I'll read the sentence and you can look at it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the text, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's the 2003 statement. There are several statements there, let me get the right one. Hold on. [Prosecution counsel confer]?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's the green tab, sir. It's the third statement down, the green tab. And the number at the top would be 2 -- 0299-2269. Would you like to take mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fourth paragraph from the bottom, do you see where it says: "A few days later," so referring to a few days after the 20th, "I heard that some prisoners had been shot at Ovcara but I don't know anything about it." Then you say: "This was more than a few days."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than a few days, maybe a period of one year, once the issue of Ovcara was raised. That's what I had in mind. So when I said a few days, it was figuratively speaking, more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you gave -- you testified in -- you testified in Belgrade, and in English it's page B92. In the B/C/S it's page 02994647, 02994647.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the usher help me find this, please? I'm looking for the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's two-thirds of the way down the page. "Q. The attorney is asking you whether you've heard about Ovcara in terms of an event that happened such as an execution of people who were captured, be it in Mitnica or elsewhere." Your answer -- do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't know about Ovcara. I heard some hints later on, but it was informal and unclear. Nobody said specifically that this had happened. After the fighting a lot of people wanted to show off and they were saying off kinds of things. One couldn't believe those stories. Some people went around boasting that they were great heroes, that they had killed so many people, and it was common knowledge that it wasn't true and that those stories should not be believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to that let's finish the next part. "When did you hear that?" And your answer is: "In a month, maybe two months before. Later, who knows what happened." When do you recall hearing, was it one month later, two months, or a few days?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember but this was back this 2004 that I gave this statement. And as to this being true, I don't know. There were stories, but I didn't know officially who or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you indicated that there were stories. People were bragging about having committed murders. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all kinds of stories in bars and so on. People were bragging and showing off about being great fighters, when in fact they were nothing. So one couldn't believe this until this was properly investigated. A lot of people boasted about being great fighters, about having done a lot, having killed a lot of people in combat. And later on one would establish that this was not the case. You know, people say all kinds of things when they're drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you indicated that there were whispers that something had happened in Ovcara. Had some people indicated that something had happened in Ovcara to make you give that testimony before the Belgrade court and also to the investigative prosecutor at Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything officially. I didn't hear from anyone. We heard that this and this had happened. I never heard this. But there were stories that something had happened in Ovcara and that people were shot. These were stories circulating in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said that there were -- you've just said that they were circulating in town. Was this in the barrooms? Was this among people talking in the streets?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you inquire further or did you just leave things alone? Did you inquire further about when people were talking about murders having occurred or about people -- prisoners being shot at Ovcara? Did you ask them what happened, who was killed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, during that period of time I was the director of a traffic company, so I was working in business. I wasn't involved in military matters. And my attitude was whatever happened there, there are military authorities that ought to investigate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in fact at that point you had been threatened yourself and you had to worry about your own life at that point. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I was replaced, as soon as I wasn't in power anymore, there were no threats anymore. As soon as I withdrew, as soon as I rejoined civilian life, there were no more threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you knew, sir, that if they would threaten you as their detachment leader -- if they would threaten to kill you, they would have no problem killing prisoners. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about it at the time, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on Friday you testified that Captain Radic looked at you with scorn on pages 11988, and you thought it might be as a result of something that Sljivancanin -- Major Sljivancanin said to him. Could you please describe how you were treated with scorn by Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now when Mr. Sljivancanin's lawyer said that I was subject of operative work, I realised what the reason was. They conducted operative work against me, they knew me, there was a media campaign against me, and Radic must have believed this. So whenever he came to the headquarters, his attitude was cold towards me. It wasn't cordial and one could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to Radic again after the date that you were replaced, the date when you were removed and Vujovic replaced you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was removed from my post, I had no further contact with them, either with Radic, with Miroljub, or with Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move briefly to another subject. You gave a statement in 1997 to the Office of the Prosecutor, which is the first document in your package, the 1997 statement, 00554903 in English. And the last paragraph, sir, you state: "In the first months after liberation of the town -- after liberation of the town was ruled by military administrators, although Executive Council of Vukovar community was nominated in mid-December." After the so-called liberation, would you agree that the town was run by a military administration?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. After the liberation the security -- the civilian authorities were not established yet. There was still military administration there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then you said that it was for the first months. So this military administration lasted for one or more months. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact period of time, but it lasted for a while after the liberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you gave your statement in 1997, were the facts fresher in your mind than today, the facts of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all of these events, I did my best to forget them, to re-enter civilian life, to spend time with my family, be devoted to my job, and be a regular citizen just like I was before the war. Had I wanted some power, they offered me to go see Milosevic, but I told them: I'm not interested in glory. I want Vukovar to be liberated. I want us to live like we lived before. I wanted to work, I was interested in my family. I wasn't interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But the question is: Would you agree that your memory was fresher back in 1997 than it -- was it fresher then when you gave your statement than today?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which events, you mean the events relating to my replacement, these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. The events of Vukovar in general.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was fresher, yes, a bit fresher, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you do not contest your earlier statement in first months after liberation of the town, and months with an "s," plural, the town was ruled by military administrators."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There was the commander of the town of Vukovar, there was that post, and then there was the town command that was supposed to re-start life in Vukovar until civilian authorities were established and took over. So there was military administration in place, and it was meant to last until civilian authorities started functioning and took over responsibilities in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, in 2003 to the Novi Sad judge, which is page L0111120, and specifically page 1125, which is page 6. In your statement to the Novi Sad judge you indicated that: "The army did not agree to civilian authorities being established immediately, saying that the conditions for that had not yet been attained and that there was a military administration in the town." Isn't that correct, the military administration remained in the town?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't have a town with no authorities. There were no civilian authorities; they hadn't been set up yet. Vukovar had been just liberated and the army withdrew, too. What do you think would have happened? There would have been marauding groups of bandits and looting and burning. There would have been a state of total lawlessness. That is what would have ensued, so it was only logical to imagine the military authorities would stay in the town until the civilian authorities were set up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just briefly one more area I want to cover. And you indicated back on Friday, it's been going for a while now, that the units, the TOs, and detachments -- local TOs and detachments were subordinated to the JNA. During this period of subordination, did you receive weapons, ammunition, clothing, hats, equipment from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had equipment on us that we had signed for in the TO, so no equipment was needed. All that was needed later on was ammunition and weapons, but we had the kit. We didn't need any more kit. Its only if our uniforms were worn out or something, so we needed new ones. But each one of us had a transport bag, a military bag, sack, and all the other kit, and each of the TO members kept these things at home. As soon as mobilised they would appear at the mobilisation point fully kitted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you would agree that ammunition, weapons were needed, hand-grenades, explosives were supplied by the JNA. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same before the war, wasn't it? The JNA was a professional army; the TO were the reserve forces. They had their own weapons, but ammunition, hand-grenades, and any other supplies were obtained from the JNA logistics bases. And that was the case under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was the JNA logistics base during the fall of 1991 where you received the supplies, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Berak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jaksic, I'll ask you several questions based on my learned friend's questions in order to clarify a couple of matters. First of all, you were asked by Mr. Weiner today and then we may go back to what was discussed last Friday. At the very beginning, page 4 of today's transcript, Mr. Weiner asked you whether there was any information in your diary about the meeting at Velepromet. And your answer was that to your knowledge there was none. My question is: What sort of diary is this? Is this really a diary or just notes in a notebook, the notebook you mentioned last Friday and which you handed over to the OTP on the weekend, of which we received copies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had kept a diary, I would have known the entire agenda for that meeting and everything that would have gone on. It would have all been written down. If there are any notes, maybe this is something outside the meeting. The same thing applies when I was at the briefing with Mr. Mrksic. The focus of the order was what I wrote down, and you have that in the diary. It's right there. If I had been at that meeting, the entire agenda would have been written down, all those present. I probably would have made notes to who said what and what conclusions were reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But my question is in relation to this. When this diary is mentioned, is it actually the notebook which you handed over to the OTP on the weekend?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the notebook. I just found it by chance. I think it was on the 17th of November, what went on. I virtually forgot what had occurred. I had virtually forgotten all about that situation. There was no need for me to remember, so I looked by chance and I chanced upon this portion about the Guards Brigade, the attack by the 5th, roughly speaking. And then after, probably, I had some sort of a pocket-sized notebook. Maybe I made some notes there, but in actual fact the orders I virtually -- well, maybe -- maybe the axes of operations or something during combat. Maybe something else was written down, maybe orders or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was: The notebook which you handed over to the OTP. Could the record be corrected that that notebook was handed over to the registry and then provided to both parties. This was not a notebook handed over to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, you corrected one of your own answers in a way today. I'm sure you will remember page 8. You talked about carrying out Mr. Mrksic's orders. You said you would have carried out any order but that this would not have applied to any orders contrary to international law of war or the Geneva Conventions. Do you remember saying that today, sir? So my question to you is: Did you ever receive any such orders from Mr. Mrksic during the relevant time while he was commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if you go back to the diary -- you see, I stopped at one point and then I underlined something in pencil that there had been this order to treat the prisoners in the spirit of the international law on war and the Geneva Conventions and this was an order of Mr. Mrksic that went to all the subordinate commanders of the units to treat the prisoners in this way. There you have it. It's right there in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are talking about making this note in the diary, and this was the order of --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, that's all very well, but my question to you was: You said you would never have carried out any orders contrary to the Geneva Conventions or international law of war. My question was: Throughout this period of time, did you in fact ever receive any such orders from Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I gave you that sort of answer. Yes, the orders -- because I'm certain that he never would have issued any such orders to begin with. And indeed, he never issued any such orders, not even close.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to one of Mr. Weiner's questions today you spoke about operative work or how you were investigated. Do you think this investigation was conducted at a time while you were still in command of the Petrova Gora TO unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was this operative work that was used to set up my removal. It was an overture, if you like, to my removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think you talked about two situations where you had a close brush with death I think?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You even specified the location. Do you think somebody was hell-bent on killing you? Is it possible, if we consider the time and place, that this was an enemy sniper, that this was a Croat sniper? Would you rule that possibility out all-together --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you've got speculative answers if that is the case, earlier. Mr. Domazet is entitled to get the matter clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first bullet, it was morning, still a bit of fog hanging in the air. Visibility was low and it whizzed right past my forehead. When you enter Velepromet just between the kitchen and the Velepromet building, it's the breadth of a gate and I thought that was that. But then later I established that our own men were holding those positions. This was the Jagodina beer factory warehouse facing Velepromet, in that area. So it could not have been enemy fire because visibility was too low, nor were they able to come that close. It could only have been organised by someone who was in a position to organise that; in other words one of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, you spoke about the meeting at Petrova Gora today, didn't you. That evening- and let me remind you, you talked about Miroljub Vujovic, who said that he had become commander and he was awaiting your reaction. Is that in reference to the day when you were told and then that evening, is this the 17th, the evening of the 17th, how does that date strike you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was before or right there or about -- well, I don't know the exact date. I don't know the exact date, but thereabouts, yes, that -- around that time, give or take a few days around the liberation of Vukovar. In actual fact, he took -- he already had -- Sljivancanin had ordered him he would be the TO commander now and that was that, end of story. It was only afterwards that he showed this decision in writing at Petrova Gora. I didn't get a copy myself, but he certainly had it and he waved it in his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's what my question was about when he showed this to you. Was that before or after the order you received on your removal, the oral order?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the order that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Weiner today at -- about the military administration after the fall of Vukovar, and you were told if there was a military administration in place for some months afterwards. And you said: Yes, at the beginning that was true and there was a town commander. First of all, do you remember who the town commander was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think there were two or three of those over a very brief period of time. There was a quick succession. I think Mr. Vojnovic was one of them. I think he was one of these town commanders, but I didn't go to the command afterwards. I did not interfere in military issues and I just don't seem to remember that. It wasn't a thing I spent a lot of time thinking about. It was only if there was a traffic-related issue I would go to the traffic industry, and I was normally in touch with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The name you just mentioned, you said it was possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was, yes, Colonel Vojnovic. I think so but I'm not 100 per cent certain; it was, just to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm looking -- because you need to make a pause because your answers come thick and fast. You're talking about Colonel Vojnovic right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were talking about Judge Vojnovic. That's not the same person, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, can you please make a pause so there's no overlap between the questions and answers. There, now we don't have that answer to my question. You were talking Judge Vojnovic and Colonel Vojnovic. Is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If not, can you tell us who the town commander was, the person you described as colonel.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic - and I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was he involved in the operations for the liberation of Vukovar? Was he a unit commander at the time? Is this something you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly wasn't at the front line, not as far as I remember. I didn't see him around there at the time or in town for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember which was the unit under his command in town after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It must have been a TO unit. Those units that were there plus the TO that had to be under that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember when the executive board or Executive Council as they called it at the time of the municipality was founded and they were supposed to be the new civilian authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I wasn't there and I don't remember. I know that there were calls for Rajko Bibic to be the chairman of the Executive Council, and I think I saw something about this later on. Later after the liberation, I don't know exactly how long after I think as much as a week, but the same question was being raised and there had been no appointment yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember if this council or members were finally appointed to this board or council by December that year?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I wasn't involved in the work of the authorities, and I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, let me ask you this, it's about something you said last Friday: He put to you the statement you gave in 2004 at the Belgrade trial, the Belgrade Ovcara trial. He spoke about 02994538. That's the document number. He spoke about that document. He suggested that Colonel Mrksic would not accept that you would carry out the duty you had been appointed to, the TO commander for the entire operations group. I'll quote your own answer on page 83 where you say -- just one correction, I said staff commander and not commander -- staff commander of the TO for Operations Group South. I'll quote a part of your own statement but where you say: "Mrksic asked for me to be only in the TO detachment. There was just one meeting and Mrksic did not allow anymore because the priority was -- and then zealots went and those others."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said one or two, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please explain this. What is it that Colonel Mrksic was opposing? You going to the meetings of the Territorial Defence of Borovo Selo? Why? For your --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He believed -- I'm sure that he believed that the Petrova Gora detachment could not go on functioning without a commander, but it's not like he had made the decision to appoint me, nor was I actually there. Those over 20 villages of -- under the operations group area who were there at the meeting and who appointed me. Mr. Mrksic said: This is a political post. Vukovar must be liberated. First we need to liberate Vukovar and then get involved in politics. He said something to this effect, first that Vukovar needed to be liberated and then following that organs of authorities had to be established, after the liberation. And the TO, the staff, and everything else, that was his opinion. These villages of the Operations Group South, they didn't have combat operations but they had their own problems. Civilian authorities weren't functioning, it had to be standardised, and life brought back to normal. This is why they established a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The TO staff did not have command authorities; its role was only to conduct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we get the question before we have an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Domazet, you'll have to repeat the question. It was lost as you turned to Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about TO staffs, you also said that the Territorial Defence was subordinated to the JNA. My question was whether the TO staff as a staff was subordinated to anyone or that was impossible, rather only that some units could be subordinated?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was subordination. Staffs could be subordinated to other staffs and units subordinated to other units. And cooperation was possible in relation to mobilisation needs and other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Here is a direct question: The TO staff, can it be subordinated to a JNA unit, to the command of a JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that I have concluded with this topic, before I turn to the next topic perhaps we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A very good idea, Mr. Domazet. We will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue, I would like to clarify a question. On Friday we showed Exhibit 269 which is a film about Velepromet on the 20th of November. We showed it to the witness, and he was able to recognise himself and some other people on this film. However, I learned that this was not admitted into evidence. It was only marked for identification during the testimony of Witness Cakalic. So could we admit 269 into evidence, please, since it hasn't been done so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a multi-part exhibit. One section concerns the meeting at Velepromet where the witness recognises himself, recognises Arkan, recognises Goran Hadzic and several -- some military people outside. There is another part of the exhibit which is another section which was taken in another city or another village which is an interview with Goran Hadzic, which the -- there is no evidence that the witness was present for. The witness had never seen it until being in court on that day. The witness could not comment upon the content of the exhibit. He said he hadn't seen it until that day in the court-room, which was page 11.963 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No need to go into the details. We know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I have no problem with the Velepromet section of the video. We would have objections to portions which are outside the knowledge of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the Prosecutor mixed two exhibits marked for identification. The other one that the Prosecutor spoke about was proposed by the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin to be admitted into evidence, which is the interview of Goran Hadzic. It was on the OTP 65 ter list, so I don't see if the OTP was the first one to propose this piece why they're objecting now. It was admitted into evidence in the Dokmanovic case as the Prosecution exhibit and I don't see why we shouldn't do the same in this trial. As to the testimony of this witness about whether he had seen this film or not, we heard from this witness that he recognised Mr. Goran Hadzic in the interview and that he had looked absolutely the same as he did on the day when the witness saw him on the government cabinet meeting on the 20th of November, 1991, at Velepromet. There is absolutely no dilemma as to what Mr. Hadzic said in that interview because the content of the interview clearly indicates that this was taken on the 20th of November, 1991, that was the date of the interview. Mr. Hadzic gave the interview after he returned from Vukovar to Sid. So I don't see that the arguments of the Prosecution are valid in this case and that they could challenge this -- these facts which are beyond dispute. And I don't see why this should not be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may contribute. This portion does not pertain to the Hadzic interview; it's quite a different exhibit. I'm only addressing Exhibit 269, which has nothing to do with the Hadzic interview that was mentioned later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, two to one at the moment. You've got exhibits mixed. Do you maintain your objection to the admission of this exhibit, this document as an exhibit? And if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to the Velepromet portion of the video, no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told there's no other portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I was just told that it's all one exhibit. It's -- just give us one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, which is the document -- the film Mr. Domazet is discussing at the moment, and the other is MFI 576.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Weiner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection to MFI 269, but we would like to object to 576 at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll leave 576 for the moment. Mr. Bulatovic has given you an opening salvo and at some time or other you will between you either reach agreement or there will be a formal motion for the admission of 576, if there is to be no more evidence to support the exhibit. Mr. Domazet, the film marked for identification as 269 will be admitted as Exhibit 269.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, we're going to carry on. In reply to my questions earlier you spoke how you had functioned at the front, not in the TO staff. My question is: While you were at the front, do you know whether the TO staff functioned properly and did all the tasks that normally fall within its purview?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff functioned in the sense that they opened the records department, they had units for identification, then they were conducting mobilisation of people outside of Vukovar in the villages in the surrounding area to ensure that people from those villages went to the front, and also mobilisation in Serbia. They opened records for that matter, and they were sending people to the front. However, this lasted for a short period of time, only one month. And one needs more time, in my view, to properly establish units and to have the staff properly up and running. So mostly they were involved in mobilisation and records pertaining to mobilisation, and it was only the commanders of units who had records about people who were actually on the front during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who conducted these tasks in the staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazo Pijevic who worked in the TO staff of Vukovar before the war, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that Uzelac was appointed staff commander. You said that he became staff commander later, but you never qualified what you meant by "later." Can you tell us that now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came sometime on the 10th of September, maybe even earlier, to Negoslavci, he came with Slobodan Grahovac to establish the staff. The staff functioned in Sid. So when the staff of the Operations Group South was established, he was appointed my deputy. And since he was the commander of the TO staff of Vukovar before the war, he knew the job really well and he was my deputy and he stood in for me while I was at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday on page 26, line 17, you said the following verbatim: "Commander and security organ were, according to the order, the authority at the time." Can you explain what you meant?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have this written down in my notebook that in the field the commander and the security organ are in charge. They are the authority. The commander from battalion level up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Today on page 30, I think, you said how you knew that sometime later Miroljub Vujovic showed a decision appointing him to the post. You also said that you didn't see him after the 20th. Therefore, did you hear this from someone? And if so, how much later after your replacement? That is to say: When did you hear that he was showing a written decision to people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was in Petrova Gora. There were Bjelic brothers there, Simo Miljanovic and it seemed weird to me that other people who were competent, reliable, decent, and honourable did not attend the meeting and that there was so very few people attending the meeting, those who were his supporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as I remember, when speaking of your replacement you said that there were no written order at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On Friday we discussed some security related questioning. You touched upon that today as well. I think that today once again you reiterated that you did not commit any abuse of your position during that period of time. Did I understand you well and do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I never allowed myself to act dishonourably to besmudge my reputation. I didn't want my children to carry that burden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While you were commander you said that daily or almost daily you went to regular briefings to Colonel Mrksic's staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a minute, let me complete my question. And that other officers were present as well. Can you tell me whether in one of those meetings you personally or your work or your orders were ever criticised either by the commander, that is to say Colonel Mrksic, or some other officer who was present at the time? Did such a thing occur prior to the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When it comes to this security investigation or some investigation that was conducted against you, can you tell us something about the reasons for that? Do you know of any reasons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to have me replaced for my command position, that was the only reason. But as to why nobody talked to me, why nobody pointed this out to me, if there were operative measures in place against me, then they were duty-bound to show me the results, the findings, of that work. If I was indeed under surveillance, then that did not affect the command functions. A commander may be replaced if a unit is at risk and only if it involves counter-intelligence work, not just some unsubstantiated rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a formal criminal complaint? Were any investigative steps taken or were any proceedings instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received any criminal complaint. I don't know of any proceedings instituted against me. If such a thing had been done, it would have gone through the General Staff and it would have reached me. If there was any blemish linked to me, then yes I would have received information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I now need to remind you that you're testifying under oath here, and as to your financial situation you said that it did not improve after the war. To the contrary, you were worse off financially after the war.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had a house in Vukovar of 330 square metres. It was fully equipped and furnished. Currently I live in a very simple house made out of mud that is not worth even one-third of my older house. I support my family, myself, through my work and farming activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the financial situation of Miroljub Vujovic before the war and after the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the family owned before the war was in his father's name; after the war he built a house which was worth 700.000 Deutschmarks plus he built a house to his father -- for his father and for his sister. So there's a totally of three houses that they own now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And when you spoke about your career after these events, I think that you mentioned that you were offered to re-join active service in the professional army, that you did so, and that you were appointed deputy commander for security affairs. In order to be appointed to that position, does one need to go through a security background check, both the person being appointed and that person's family? And could somebody be appointed to that post if there was anything murky in their past, any blemish in their past?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. One could not be appointed to any such position if they had any blemish in their past or any disciplinary or any other infraction, even if it was a matter of a simple, ordinary crime, let alone something committed while in military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "ordinary crime," you mean --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian, in civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you were both appointed professional officer and later on you were a security officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jaksic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions which have been asked of you. Your evidence is at an end, and you are now free to return to your home and normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance you've been able to give us. Thank you, and the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all. Our next witness is Mr. Dusan Milosevic. He should be in the building and I think we will be seeing him very soon. I would just like to take advantage of this time while we're waiting for the witness to familiarise the Chamber with some facts. In relation to the continuation of our Defence case and to see what awaits us over the following period so that both the Chamber and my learned friends from the OTP could take that into account. First and foremost, I wish to inform everyone that Mr. Mrksic's Defence has decided to drop our military expert and his report, who will now not be appearing. So that's one witness less. As things stand right now - and here I'm including the witness who is about to appear - we shall be hearing another three or four witnesses. One will be arriving tomorrow evening, and the one after him, I hope, will be here by the end of the week. In addition to these two witnesses, we have another witness in relation to whom there has been a court ruling and I expect him to be arriving in The Hague early next week. There's the fourth witness in relation to whom another subpoena has been issued, but there may be problems with that witness. So I move that we go private session briefly, Your Honours. We want to know what the position of the Chamber is on this witness so that we can plan our own time and the conclusion of our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the diary of the last witness has been held by the court officer so far. Is it proposed by any counsel to seek to tender it? I think its time has gone and counsel have seen it. Well, given the silence, it will be able to be released to the witness. Now, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour. Mr. Lunny will be handling this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir, would you be kind enough to take the card and read aloud the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, all. Good afternoon, sir. Can you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we speak the same language and both my questions and your answers are being interpreted for everyone to understand what we are talking about. Therefore, please make a short pause after each of my questions before you embark on your answer in order to allow the interpreters sufficient time to do their work. I think the best course of action might be for you to follow the cursor on the monitor. When you see the cursor stop, when you see a sentence end, please start your answer.
