Sir, what is your profession? Tell us about your education and your work experience.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am a pilot. I was trained at the reserve officers' school for the air force in Zadar, later in Tuzla. And I joined active service later on as a pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In 1991, which is the year that we are looking at in this trial, where were you serving and what types of planes were you flying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was serving at Batajnica airport, the 890th Mixed Helicopters Squadron. I flew the following helicopters: H-42 and H-45, the Gazelles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say "H-42" and "H-45," Gazelle, can you explain what this is about. Are these two different varieties of the helicopter type or are they entirely different helicopters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They're essentially the same helicopter, but they have two different types of engine. The H-42 has a 3B engine and the H-45 has 114M, which is a more powerful engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Back in 1991, did your squadron have a mission related to the activities of the Guards Motorised Brigade in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please be so kind as to tell us about the type of mission that this was.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was about transport and about medical transport; that means we flew passengers and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which helicopter types and which numbers were used for this mission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a permanent presence of two helicopters, one was a transport helicopter, HD-40, and there was an H-45 Gazelle. Those two were always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say "HD40," can you tell us the brand of this helicopter, the make?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nijos [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: About the transcript, page 54, line 10, it's M-i-o-s [as interpreted], that's the name of the helicopter. Yes, M-i-8. That's right, thank you. What was the Gazelle helicopter used for in the Vukovar area back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Gazelle was used to ferry the Guards Brigade commander, Mr. Mile Mrksic. When he didn't need the helicopter, he allowed the helicopter to be used for the transport of those wounded most in need of being taken as quickly as possible to the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Negoslavci, which of the two tasks was more typical, was it to transport the commander or the wounded in Gazelle?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We transported the wounded more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in order to transport the wounded in the Gazelle helicopter, did one need to make any changes in the equipment of the helicopter or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A minimum modification was needed. One needed to take out the left seat and then also the feet command that are on the left side needed to be removed, and then one could fit in a stretcher in the back, towards the left seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when a wounded person is transported in the helicopter and when the seat is removed as you described to us, who mans the helicopter in such a case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In such a case there is a pilot and a medical escort manning the helicopter; most often it's a doctor and sometimes it's a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is that different from the typical crew composition manning such a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Usually when one is involved in a different tasks, there is a pilot and a technician as crew members on the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the relevant period of time, pilots performed these duties for the Guards Brigade. Were the pilots constantly present in the area where the Guards Brigade was positioned or billeted or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, not all the time. We would have shifts lasting three to four days, so we would rotate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will need the assistance of the usher to distribute these hard copies of Exhibit 764, which we already saw in the court-room. Could one copy please be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have before you a document admitted into evidence as Exhibit 764. Can you tell us what this document represents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the log-book of flights of 890th Helicopter Squadron for Gazelles, H-45 and HD-40.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us how information is recorded in this log-book. What is the standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Information is entered into log-book based on the flight plan. Following a completion of a mission, a pilot normally records certain information related to that flight, distance, number of hours, briefly itinerary, and how many passengers, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that a pilot normally records this in the flight plan. Where is the flight plan typically located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The flight plan can be found in the office of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that in this case the flight plan was located in Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please explain to me something further. Once this information is entered into the flight plan, how is this information then transferred into the flight log-book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Upon being recorded in the flight plan, usually one of junior pilots tasked with this -- perhaps just somebody with a nice handwriting copies this from the plan into the flight log-book. Most often this is done by junior pilots or somebody who wasn't flying at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in relation to how -- or rather, to when this is recorded in the flight plan, can you tell us how much time usually elapses before the information is copied from the plan into the log-book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This doesn't even have to be done immediately after completing a flight. It can be done on the following day or after several days. If a pilot is somewhere in the field, then they would wait for him to come back to report on flights completed. They would wait for him to return to his unit before this information is then copied in the flight log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 01D0400, 1D040081. What is recorded for the 14th of November, 1991? Do you see somewhere any indication about you flying on that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, helicopter H-42 from Batajnica to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember why you flew on that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I went to take my shift. I was due to take over my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. It was your shift duty. Are the flights taken on the following days recorded in this log-book, the flights that you did in Negoslavci on the following days?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th, 16th, 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and tell us when you flew, the date; tell us about your destination, the aircraft; and if you remember, who you transported.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, 15th, 16th, and 17th.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th in the afternoon hours, it says here 1400 hours, I transported from Negoslavci to the military medical academy a wounded British journalist. Mr. Mile Mrksic approved and in fact ordered us to transport the journalist in his helicopter. If I remember, his first name was David.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, what does it say about the aircraft you flew and what was your destination?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I flew in H-45 Gazelle, number 893. Itinerary: Negoslavci military medical academy, Batajnica, where I refueled. And then I went back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you fly on the 16th of November; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th I flew from Negoslavci to Dalj. I transported Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Pavkovic to a meeting with General Panic. And then I went back to the same starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That was on the 16th of November, 1991. What aircraft you flew? Where did you take off from and where did you land?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The aircraft was Gazelle H-45, registration number 893. I took off from Negoslavci, landed in Dalj, and then again my sortie was from Dalj and my destination was Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the 17th of November, 1991, did you fly; and if so, which aircraft and which destination? And, if you remember, who did you transport?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of November, I flew again in Gazelle H-45, same registration number, 893. My itinerary was Negoslavci medical military academy; Batajnica, where I refueled; and then I went back to Negoslavci. I was transporting a wounded person who needed urgent medical attention. The second flight was in the late afternoon hours. Again I flew in the same helicopter a wounded patient to the military medical academy, but the weather was very difficult. I was unable to reach the military medical academy. I landed on the Heliodrom of police in Novi Sad, and I left my patient there because there is a hospital in Novi Sad as well. I stayed the night in Novi Sad due to inclement weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about your recollections for the 18th? Would you please look at what is recorded in the log-book for the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 18th I was supposed to be relieved by my colleague Pantovic. I called the command of the squadron from Novi Sad and I was told to fly from Novi Sad to Batajnica in order for somebody else to take up the shift. That's what I did. My colleague Pantovic took over my helicopter and he flew to Negoslavci in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where was the rotation supposed to take place anyway and which helicopter were you flying in on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The rotation was to take place in Negoslavci; however, since I was already in Novi Sad due to practical reasons, in order to save on the fuel, to be economical with our resources, I was told by the squadron command to go to Batajnica so that Pantovic could take over the helicopter and fly to Negoslavci in order to avoid duplicating flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the aircraft. Which one were you in when you came from Negoslavci -- from Novi Sad to Batajnica and when Pantovic took over the helicopter to fly to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was Gazelle H-45, registration number 893.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you find the next record of you piloting a helicopter, as recorded in this flight log-book. Tell us which day it was, which aircraft.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 22nd of November. The aircraft was Gazelle H-45, registration number 892, and I flew from Batajnica to Dedinje, where I stayed for two hours waiting for Mr. Mile Mrksic in order to fly him to Negoslavci. Major Tesic was with him. Then once we took off for Negoslavci, we reached Fruska Gora and the weather once again was very bad. It was difficult for us to continue with our flight. I tried to cross the Danube, but I was unable due to inclement weather. I returned to Batajnica; I landed there. We waited there until 1300 hours, at which time they reported to us from Negoslavci that the weather improved; however, from Batajnica one can see Fruska Gora and we could see that the clouds were still low. So at 1300 hours we flew to Negoslavci, we landed there. Major Tesic and Colonel Mrksic disembarked, and I returned back to Batajnica. My colleague, Mr. Novicevic had taken over with his own helicopter already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you say that Mr. Novicevic was in Negoslavci with his own helicopter when you landed. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was already there when I landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: First of all, the entry in relation to the 22nd of November, it says Batajnica-Dedinje, and then the flight was interrupted -- or rather, work was interrupted. And then again Batajnica-Negoslavci-Batajnica. What does this note mean, work interrupted or flight interrupted, what does that mean, that sort of an entry, what does that tell us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Flight interrupted means you can't complete a flight for a variety of reasons. If your equipment is broken, if the weather conditions are inclement, or sometimes the pilot or one of the crew can get sick as well. There are all sorts of reasons. In this case, it was about the weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where exactly where you caught by this bad weather and where did you land to wait for the weather to clear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was caught by the bad weather at Fruska Gora, roughly speaking, at the Banco pass. I decided to fly back to Batajnica because it was relatively close. We decided not to wait in a place that wasn't safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please look at the log and tell us which helicopter you flew on that day, the 22nd of November, 1991? What's the helicopter number?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was an H-45, a Gazelle, and the registration number is 892.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you took off from Batajnica and were off to Dedinje on this helicopter. Can you please look at the previous entry in relation to Gazelle 892 in this log. According to this entry, where is this helicopter at this time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The helicopter in relation to the 21st of November, 1991, the pilot was Novicevic and the route was Batajnica-Topcider-Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on what you just told us, the helicopter should be in Negoslavci, right, but you're telling us that you took off in this helicopter on the 22nd from Batajnica. Are you certain that this was the same helicopter? If so, how do you explain this entry in the log?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am certain. I am certain it was this helicopter that I used. This was a scheduled flight during working hours. I think this must be misrecorded. I think Pantovic flew back on 892 from Negoslavci to Batajnica and took off the same day at 1130 hours. So Novicevic was left with the 893, which was a helicopter that was normally kept at Negoslavci because it had the most powerful engine and the best helicopter for us to use, the newest model as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that specific day, do you remember the 892 landing in Belgrade and the 893 landing in Negoslavci? Or is your memory based on the fact that, as you have just indicated, the more powerful helicopter was normally kept at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My memory is based on the fact that I remember us keeping the 893. The helicopter technicians told us that this was the best helicopter to keep there, to keep there in the field. I think this is an erroneous entry. Novicevic came on 21st on the 892; he arrived in Negoslavci at 0840 hours. And Pantovic took off from Negoslavci at 1130 hours on the 892 and flew back to Batajnica, leaving Novicevic with the 893.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at this log. Find the entries between the 14th and the 24th of November. Wherever there's a reference to the 893, can you please read for each of the days where the helicopter was, what was the location of the helicopter, which heliport, if you would be so kind, sir. I'm talking about the 893.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't see it on the 14th. On the 15th I was the pilot, Negoslavci medical military academy, Batajnica-Negoslavci. I was ferrying the English journalist. On the 16th I was the pilot. Negoslavci-Dalj and back, Dalj to Negoslavci. I was flying Colonel Mrksic. On the 17th it was me again; Negoslavci medical military academy, Batajnica-Negoslavci. The afternoon of the same day, Negoslavci to Novi Sad where I landed due to inclement weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. The Negoslavci-Novi Sad flight, according to the flight schedule, where was the flight supposed to begin and where was it supposed to end had it not been for inclement weather?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The flight was supposed to begin in Negoslavci, as indeed it did. It was supposed to end at the medical military academy, but I was caught by nightfall and we did not have any night-time landings in Negoslavci. So I just landed in Batajnica to sit and wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Had this not been about transporting wounded persons, so this was a flight early in the evening, and bearing in mind the fact that there was a change of shift for the pilots, where would you have handed over to Pantovic, at which point, in which place on this flight on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to hand over to him in Negoslavci, had things gone according to plan, but I was caught by bad weather in Novi Sad, which is relatively close to Batajnica. I was ordered by the squadron command to fly back to Batajnica and lie low.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is the 893, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your colleague Mr. Pantovic, based on this log, where did he take the helicopter on the 18th of November? Where did he park it on his way out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He took it from Batajnica airport and flew to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Looking at all these dates that you have been telling us about, the 15th, the 16th, the 17th, and the 18th -- my apologies. First of all -- sir, first of all, can you please tell me at the end of these days where was the 893 on all of these days at day's end, which heliport?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you mean the entries in this log-book, this is the 24th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, just a minute, please. I asked you -- you've read out all these entries to us, the 14th, the 15th, the 16th, the 17th, the 18th, where did the 893 take off from and where did it land on each of these days? You read this out to us. Is it always the same place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All the landings were in Negoslavci as well as all the take-offs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the 24th of November a while ago. Can you please be so kind and read the entry in relation to the 24th. Who was flying, which helicopter, and what was the route?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 24th of November, the pilot was Novicevic. The helicopter was the 893. The route was Negoslavci-Mladenovo and Mladenovo-Negoslavci. And then Negoslavci-Dedinje-Batajnica-Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 24th is the day the Guards Brigade returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a good time for our second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before the break you read out the location of the 893. You said it took off from Negoslavci and it landed back in Negoslavci; right? Can you please now use the same log-book and see about the 892, where it took off from on a certain day and where it landed, having completed its mission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What certain day, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like the witness to read the references in relation to all these days between the 14th and the 22nd of November, which was the last flight of that particular helicopter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of November the 892 flew Batajnica-Negoslavci at 0930 hours, and the return at 1415 hours Negoslavci to Batajnica. That's the 892. The 15th of November, 1991, Batajnica-Ladjevci airport near Kraljevo and then back to Batajnica. The 16th, no entry. The 17th, no entry. Again, on the 19th of November, Batajnica-Kovin and back, Kovin-Batajnica. And then the entry on the 21st, 0800 hours, Batajnica, Topcider, Negoslavci. And the 22nd Batajnica-Dedinje, mission interrupted, Batajnica-Negoslavci-Batajnica, although I believe that this flight on the 21st at 1130 hours was done using the 892. The 893 reflects an erroneous entry. I think whoever recorded this made an error. It must have been a slip.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, based on all these entries that you have just read out, can we conclude that the 892 was always returned to Batajnica heliport on each of these days?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, 1991, do you remember where you found these helicopters and where did you take off from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Outside the hangar at Batajnica airport, that's where I took it. I flew over to Dedinje, where I waited for about two hours. I took off again. I flew to Fruska Gora. I couldn't get through. I turned around, flew back to Batajnica, and waited until 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained that. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which aircraft did you fly on the 22nd of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A helicopter, an H-45 Gazelle, registration number 892.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one more thing. Can you please look at the entry for the 21st of November, 1991, the entry in this log. Is there an entry in relation to a flight between 8.00 and 8.30 in the morning, the take-off between 8.00 and 8.30 in the morning from Negoslavci to Belgrade, that is Batajnica? Was there a flight like that that was recorded?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no such flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With great satisfaction, no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic. I have a few questions for you now on the evidence you have given. First of all, with regard to the morning of the 22nd when you collected Colonel Mrksic and Major Tesic from Dedinje, you said you had to fly there and wait for them for a period of time. When you were waiting there, did you see these two men arriving at the heliport?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was waiting for them at the headquarters of the Guards Brigade in the canteen. I was drinking coffee with some other officers and my mechanic Nikolic was with me, Staff Sergeant First Class Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Did you see -- if the answer to this is no, just say no. But did you see Colonel Mrksic arriving at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him at the headquarters that morning several times briefly. He had some business there and he told us to wait for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: There's perhaps some confusion with -- through the translation. But did you see him actually arrive at the headquarters that morning? For example, did you see him arriving by a car?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was at the headquarters already by the time we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can move on then from that aspect to Exhibit 764 which you already have before you, Mr. Milosevic, being the flight log. As I understand it from your evidence, you were not responsible for the completion of any of these entries in this book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't responsible. I was a mere pilot. I had no command responsibilities. As for what was recorded, the entries were made by junior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With regard to the entries being made by junior officers, if I said to you this Court had heard evidence that those entries were later checked by the squad commander or the squad commander's deputies, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would, but errors are always possible. I don't think a major error would be possible, such as the omission of entire flight or a pilot suddenly being logged who didn't actually fly on that day. But a helicopter registration number, I think a slip in that department would be possible. One thing I would like to add is regarding the technical documentation of each helicopter, each helicopter has a maintenance booklet in which information is entered. When a helicopter is due for maintenance, for checks, information is used from this maintenance record which is added too after every flight that a helicopter makes, and that is reliable, not the flight log itself. The technician, for example, does not take into account the flight log but information from the maintenance record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're obviously several steps ahead of me. I've not yet asked you about flights being omitted; I simply asked you about whether or not the entries were double-checked and you said they were. And is it the case then that these entries were double-checked because this log was an important document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were checked, but errors are always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Milosevic, you're not answering the question you've been asked, which was: These entries are double-checked because this is an important document. Yes or no, is this an important document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I told you that this Court had heard evidence describing the document as a high-precision log because of the information contained within it, would you agree with that description of the log?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a high-precision document since there's an obvious error in relation to the 21st, which would affect the 22nd and the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If we can then move on to that error of the 21st, which I think - unless I'm wrong, Mr. Milosevic - in the B/C/S version is page 0083 and in the English translation 0089. Do you have that in front of you, sir, the entry for the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you've confirmed for us already you were not responsible for those entries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And with regards to your answers to my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, on each occasion when you referred to the error you started it with "I think," "I think there was an error." "I think it was erroneous." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how else to put it. I wasn't present at all times and in every place. It's just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So regardless of your thoughts, you don't actually know what the error was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I look at the log I see there's an error in relation to the 21st because the 892 returned to Batajnica at 1130 hours instead of the 893. The 893 remained in Negoslavci throughout and was being used by pilot Novicevic, who was on the shift at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And from that you have simply surmised that the error is one of typing or entry rather than anything else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, an error regarding this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: However, Mr. Milosevic, if we start with the 21st of November with helicopters 893 and 892 and if we work back the way, we see further up the page relating to the 18th and 19th of November, if I can deal first with the 18th of November, helicopter 893 starts the -- sorry, finishes the day in Negoslavci. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And helicopter 892 finishes the day in Batajnica - is that not also correct - on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 19th. On the 18th, the 892 did not fly. On the 19th, the 892 flew Batajnica-Kovin and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And that, Mr. Milosevic, would also -- or does tie in with the entry of the 21st, which says that the 893 started in Negoslavci and the 892 started in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you look at this, the take-off at Batajnica occurred at 8.00, and the take-off from Negoslavci occurred at 1130. Pilot Novicevic's shift was starting on that day, so he took the 892 and he flew to Negoslavci. Pilot Pantovic returned to Batajnica on the same helicopter once his shift was over. You see that the first flight chronologically, the first flight was recorded below the chronologically later flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that, however, the starting point for each helicopter is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Perhaps this is my error, and if it is I apologise, but that mean then not only the numbers are wrong but where the helicopters flew between is also wrong?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The route was correct. I remember when Pantovic returned from Negoslavci to Batajnica. I was present and we had a chat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If one were to look at this document simply on the face of it and looking at the 21st of November and the 22nd of November, it would appear that helicopter 893 finished in Batajnica on the 21st and 892 finished in Negoslavci on the 21st. You would agree with me, purely from the face of the document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Helicopter 892 was the only one that flew on the 21st. The 893 remained in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'm not asking about what you think may have happened, as you said in your evidence in chief; I'm asking you about what is recorded in the document itself. And in the document itself we have 893 finished in Batajnica and 892 finished in Negoslavci. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the document, but it is an evident mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: However, with regard to the 22nd of November, 892 starts in Batajnica. And again from the face of the document, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was available in Batajnica. And on that day, I flew it within the working hours. It wasn't my shift, but I flew it during business hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: However, again on the face of the document, not what you think may have happened, but on the face of the document there is nothing to show how helicopter 892 finished in Negoslavci at 8.40 in the morning of the 21st and then leaves Batajnica at 8.00 a.m. on the morning of the 22nd. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question entirely. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Indeed. You've agreed already that on the face of the document flight 892 is recorded as finishing the night at Negoslavci on the 21st. You agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it took off at 11.30 to Batajnica --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'm not asking, Mr. Milosevic, about what you think is the error because the document, as you've agreed, says that flight 893 took off -- I'm not interested in what you think happened and what you think was the error. But on the face of it, this important document that was double-checked by commanders has the 892 finishing in Negoslavci and not leaving Negoslavci thereafter. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. What do you mean the -- how come I flew on the 22nd then?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The document -- purely the document -- if someone is looking at this document on its own, not the pilot who thinks he can remember 15 years ago what the numbers were and what the error might be, but someone reading this document would find out from this document that 892 came from Batajnica via Topcider and finished at Negoslavci. And from the 21st -- from the entry in the 21st as it is in the log itself, as typed up -- or written in, rather, it doesn't leave again according to the log. I'm not interested in what you think may have happened; I'm interested in what the log itself records.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what's written in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that doesn't correspond to reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You didn't -- after you said your memory, you think, and we're going back 15 years, Mr. Milosevic, but with regard to the log you've agreed that that's what the log discloses. And if we then go to the 22nd of November, the same log, described by you as important I think -- or rather, you accepted it was important and was double-checked by the commanders at headquarters, that has 892 leaving Batajnica purely as a matter of record. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat which date you had in mind. I don't understand which date this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: On the morning of the 22nd, helicopter 892 is recorded in the log as leaving from Negoslavci, just as a matter of record from that log. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what my learned friend said is not written in this log-book, that on the 22nd 892 took off from Negoslavci; rather, it says that it took off from Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply a slip of the tongue. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'm obliged to my learned friend for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: For the 22nd of November, the log shows 892 leaving Batajnica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, there's nothing on the face of the log - and again, I'm not interested in what you think the error was - but on the face of the log there is no entry to explain how helicopter 892 got from Negoslavci on the evening of -- or on the day of 1991 -- 21st of November, 1991, to be in Batajnica on the morning of 22nd of November, 1991. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The explanation is that on the 21st pilot Pantovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could please stop you, Mr. Milosevic. Again, my question is not directed as to what you think the explanation is; my question is directed as to what the log discloses as a matter of fact, that there is nothing on that page on the face of the document alone to describe how helicopter 892 got from Negoslavci on the 21st to Batajnica on the 22nd. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Helicopter 892 returned on the 21st to Batajnica. The only explanation possible is that there was error in the entry. You say that the commanders check the log-book. Nothing was crossed out here --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- or revised. And it is possible that they failed to notice the mistake, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But again, Mr. Milosevic, you have not answered the question you have been asked. With regard to the document itself, there is no explanation within the document about the discrepancy of where the helicopters are?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Helicopter 892 on the 21st took off at 8.00, flying to Batajnica and returned at 11.30 from Negoslavci to Batajnica. It took off at 8.00 from Batajnica and at 11.30 it returned to Batajnica. Whoever made this entry made an erroneous entry as to the registration number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can stop you there, Mr. Milosevic. Regardless of the question you're being asked, you appear to have a mantra in reply, you appear to have a fixed answer. Regardless of what you're asked about the log-book, you seem to only want to reply about what you think was the error. Now, if I suggest to you that there was a flight on the morning of the 21st of November that was not logged in the diary, whether by error or by deceit, how would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't see this as possible. I'm sure that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No pilot would allow for his flight not to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is that an absolute rule, that no pilot would allow for a flight not to be recorded?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't, and I'm sure the same is true of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Milosevic, that would apply to every single flight you flew, you would record every single flight, no matter how short, no matter how insignificant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I always recorded all of my flights because that reflected the hours that I flew during my career, and that's a very important information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The very important information you've referred to, hours flying, does that also apply to location where you flew from and where you flew to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's important, too. Sometimes people record even locations where they do not land, but rather make U-turns in air.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Can we look then for the entry of the 22nd of November, then. It's page 0089 on the English version and 0083 on the B/C/S version, Mr. Milosevic. Do you have that in front of you still?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And forgive me if I'm wrong, but we have the first entry of the 892 flying from Batajnica to Dedinje from 8.00 in the morning and you landed at ten past 8.00, a flight of ten minutes' duration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The next reference to any location is Batajnica, which is two lines down, where you'd recorded the flight from Batajnica to Negoslavci and back to Batajnica. That is also correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But there are no details of the flight from Dedinje to Batajnica, there are no details of taking off, when you took off -- or rather, the 10.00 entry, is that when you took off from Dedinje?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 10.00 flight? Yes, I took off from Dedinje. I flew to the slopes of Fruska Gora. I came to the Bancvo pass, but I couldn't continue due to inclement weather, and I decided to return to Batajnica to wait for the weather to improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But the actual start point and end point of that flight are not recorded in the log-book, are they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they're not. The rule is to simply write down, "flight interrupted," if that is what took place. So that's what we wrote down, "flight interrupted."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So if your flight was interrupted and you ended up at a different airport from the one you left, there would be no record of starting point and finishing point?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that case it would have been recorded. For example, if there was a change in an airport, but Dedinje is also in Batajnica region and Fruska Gora itself also is in proximity -- is in close proximity to the Batajnica airport. All of these locations are close.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But again, on the face of this document and in the face of those entries, there's no reference to a flight between Dedinje and Batajnica, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not mentioned here in this line, but if you look in the following line you can see that the aircraft took off from Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If we move away now from the log-book itself, Mr. Milosevic, and now I'm asking you just a few general questions about your flying as a helicopter pilot. In the course of your career, were you ever asked to fly forensic teams or police investigative teams to investigate any criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not any of your colleagues were involved in flying forensic teams to investigate criminal allegations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: In the last week of November 1991 and to December 1991, were you and your squadron available to fly forensic teams had you been asked to do so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about others. As for me, in early December 1991, I had a flight to Podgorica transporting the crew of a Canadair aircraft, and I think that that's all as far as my activities in 1991 are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I apologise I took longer than anticipated, perhaps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lunny. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My learned friend cross-examined the witness in detail, so I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you this: These records about the flight, are they recorded only in this log-book or perhaps in some other documents as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat? I wasn't concentrated there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We spoke about the flights recorded in the log-book. Let me ask you, are these flights recorded also in some personal documents of pilots?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The flights are recorded in the flight record book or booklet, and this is done on a daily basis. The entries made reflect number of flights, number of hours and minutes, but there is no information as to the location of take-off and landing. In addition to this, there is the annual book of flights where all flights are added up, all flights taken during a year, and classified based on the type of assignment. This is all recorded in this booklet, including the type of skills that the pilot has.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend you answered about flights that perhaps were not recorded. In your career, did you ever hear of any flight not recorded in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I never heard that. Every pilot takes great care to ensure that his flights are recorded, even if these were just five-minute flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for this witness. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the flight recorded on the 24th of November, 1991, the last flight of the day in H-45, 893, where did it finish?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you referred to it earlier, you said it finished in Negoslavci. I just wanted to correct that. Can you tell me who in your pilots had the initials A. K. L.?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A. K. L., these are the initials for air traffic control at the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I ask you that question because the log-book you're looking at appears to have at the top of each page a date and then aircraft leader, A.K.L. This wouldn't be a log maintained by air traffic control, would it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of logs air traffic control had, but each squadron supplied its records to the air traffic control as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But this log is one maintained by your squadron, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Who was A.K.L., can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: See here, when training is conducted, training flights, where it says "leader of flights," some of the pilots, usually squadron commander, his deputy, navigation assistant, or some other senior pilots are designated as flight leaders to be next to air-traffic controller if any assistance is needed by the pilot. Since all of these flights were unscheduled flights, nor flight leader was designated; rather, the air-traffic control plays that role, that of flight leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the designation A.K.L. in each case is simply a reference to air-traffic control?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding that the entries you say were made by -- in this log were made by a junior officer who was not flying on the day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question. I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood from your evidence that you said that this log is normally made up by a junior officer who is not flying.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They mostly copy this information from the flight plan. They would simply copy it from the flight plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that's a job not done by the same officer, but whoever is available to do it; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's mostly the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The original handwritten log appears to be entirely in the same handwriting. Is that correct? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That does seem to apply to this particular day, but it's possible that the information was copied without really doing it on an everyday basis when a efficient number of flight plans had been accumulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the entries from the 14th of November to the 24th of November, ten days, although not all of them had entries. Would you agree they appear to be the same hand?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They appear to be, yes. I'm not an expert myself, but I would certainly say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The one page that's different appears to be the last page which is the summary, as I read it, for the month of November.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to judge the handwriting. It may have been a recording made later on, not the same day, and maybe it was made by someone else. But it's very difficult for me to judge. I'm really no expert in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the entries that are here, it would appear there were no flights after the 24th of November for the remainder of November by the squadron. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We would conclude any given month by the 25th in the air force. So everything -- all the flights made after the 25th of November were, for purely administrative purposes, taken as December flights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll be pleased to know that concludes the questions for you. You're now free to return to your ordinary affairs. We would like to thank you for your attendance here and the assistance that you've been able to give. So you're now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears we must now adjourn until Wednesday in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask something, if possible. Thank you. Our witness Lesanovic is arriving tomorrow on the evening flight through Vienna. This is a witness who was the chief of the anti-aircraft defence of the Guards Brigade in Operations Group South. I think we shall have to proof him overnight and he would be extremely tired the next morning and we won't have sufficient time to proof him on all the subjects. Therefore, I would like to ask, if possible, to start his testimony on Thursday morning in order to have adequate time for him to rest upon arrival and in order for us to be able to proof him on all the details that we believe to be relevant, also for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That means, Mr. Vasic, that we must be entirely sure of concluding that witness by Friday. So that means you're going to have to take less than your estimated time of four hours, to be sure of allowing adequate time for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. We shall do our best to focus on what is important to us within the given time. And I am certain that we can finish the witness by the end of Friday -- not just we in the sense of the Mrksic Defence team, but rather all the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will, Mr. Vasic. We will ask you tomorrow morning to make contact with the Chamber's Senior Legal Officer, Ms. Chifflet, to ensure that the matter of the witnesses that you want to arrive under subpoena can be followed up as quickly as possible. Because quite obviously there is no time to spare at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. This is really in our best interest. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn now until Thursday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.53 p.m.,
